title: Fiber Double Buffering (WorkInProgress Tree Cloner)
concept: Double Buffering & Pointer Flipping in Commit Phase
problemStatement: Implement `createWorkInProgress(currentFiber, pendingProps)` that creates or reuses the `alternate` Fiber node. It must clone the current node into its alternate, update `pendingProps`, link their mutual `alternate` references, and return the workInProgress node.
interviewTrap: Re-allocating new objects on every render causes GC churn. React reuses the existing `current.alternate` node whenever available to maintain peak performance.

testCases.name: Creates new alternate and links mutual references
testCases.testFn: const current = { tag: 'Host', type: 'div', memoizedProps: {}, alternate: null }; const wip = createWorkInProgress(current, { id: 'wip' }); return current.alternate === wip && wip.alternate === current;

testCases.name: Reuses existing alternate on subsequent renders (zero new object allocation)
testCases.testFn: const current = { tag: 'Host', type: 'div', memoizedProps: {}, alternate: null }; const wip1 = createWorkInProgress(current, { count: 1 }); const wip2 = createWorkInProgress(current, { count: 2 }); return wip1 === wip2 && wip2.pendingProps.count === 2;

testCases.name: Updates pendingProps while preserving memoizedProps until commit
testCases.testFn: const current = { tag: 'Host', type: 'div', memoizedProps: 'old', alternate: null }; const wip = createWorkInProgress(current, 'new'); return { pending: wip.pendingProps, memoized: wip.memoizedProps };

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React utilizes a Double Buffering pooling strategy to avoid constant object allocations during re-renders. At any time, there are at most two trees: the `current` tree (rendered on screen) and the `workInProgress` (WIP) tree (being constructed in memory). They mirror each other via `alternate` pointers.
stepByStepWalkthrough: - If `null`, instantiate a new Fiber node `workInProgress`, set `workInProgress.alternate = current` and `current.alternate = workInProgress`.
- If `alternate` exists (from previous render pass), recycle it! Copy updated `pendingProps`, reset `flags = 0`, `subtreeFlags = 0`, and copy over pointers.
Return recycled or newly allocated `workInProgress` fiber.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiber.js`, `createWorkInProgress` recycles existing fibers instead of allocating new JS objects on every render. This dramatically reduces V8 Heap garbage collection churn during frequent updates (e.g. 60fps animations or typing).

complexity.time: O(1) constant time per fiber clone/recycle operation.
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary allocation (reuses alternate fiber once instantiated).

edgeCasesHandled: Initial render creates alternate and binds bidirectional link (`a.alternate = b` and `b.alternate = a`).
Subsequent renders reuse existing alternate object without GC allocation.
WorkInProgress resets mutation flags to clean slate.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Explain the Double Buffering pattern in React Fiber.
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: React maintains at most two Fiber trees at any given time: 1) `current`: the tree currently rendered and visible on screen. 2) `workInProgress` (WIP): the tree being constructed and diffed in memory during the render phase. When work completes and is committed to the DOM, React simply flips a single root pointer: `fiberRoot.current = workInProgress`. The previous `current` tree becomes the pool for the next render's `workInProgress`, completely recycling fiber objects via the `alternate` pointer.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: The foundational memory management concept in React Fiber architecture.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How does createWorkInProgress avoid object allocation churn?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: In `ReactFiber.js`, `createWorkInProgress(current, pendingProps)` checks if `current.alternate` already exists from a prior render. If it exists, React recycles that exact object: it resets `flags = NoFlags`, copies `pendingProps`, and reuses its existing memory allocation instead of calling `new FiberNode()`. This reduces V8 heap garbage collection pressure during rapid typing or animations.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests understanding of JIT memory optimization in hot UI paths.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: What happens to the workInProgress tree if an update is aborted or superseded by higher-priority work?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: If higher-priority work (like user typing) interrupts low-priority work (like data fetching), React simply abandons the `workInProgress` pointer. Because no mutations have touched the host DOM (which only occurs during commit), discarding WIP leaves the visible `current` tree 100% intact with zero visual tearing.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Highlights the core superpower of Double Buffering in Concurrent Mode.

realWorldUseCases.description: While a large table renders in a background transition, keystrokes discard incomplete WIP trees and render immediately without lag.
realWorldUseCases.companies: Notion Web, Linear, Google Sheets Web

howToExplain.opening: React uses graphics-style Double Buffering: it diffs changes on an in-memory workInProgress tree, and atomically flips the root pointer to commit changes to the screen.
keyPoints: current tree represents what is on screen; workInProgress represents the next frame.
Alternate pointers link corresponding nodes bidirectionally.
Discarding WIP work produces zero screen artifacts (tear-free abortability).
Recycles existing fiber objects to prevent V8 garbage collection stutter.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Double buffering gives React the transactional safety of a database: renders can abort cleanly, or commit atomically in a single pointer swap.
analogies: A theater stage with two rotating platforms: the audience watches actors on Stage A (current) while crew members assemble the next set on Stage B (WIP) behind the curtain; when ready, the stage rotates instantly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking React allocates a brand new Fiber tree on every setState.
commonMistakes.why: React recycles the existing alternate fibers. At any time, there are at most 2 fiber instances per component.
commonMistakes.correct: State that React caps memory to two trees and reuses alternate fibers.

followUpDeepDive.question: Where in React source does the atomic root pointer swap occur?
followUpDeepDive.answer: In `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js` inside `commitRootImpl()`, immediately after `commitMutationEffects` finishes and before `commitLayoutEffects`: `root.current = finishedWork;`.
